verses.text: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple.
Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew.
One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”
The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke.
Then I said, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies!”
Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar.
He touched my mouth with it, and said, “Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven.”
I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am. Send me!”
He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’

Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
Then I said, “Lord, how long?” He answered, “Until cities are waste without inhabitant, and houses without man, and the land becomes utterly waste,
And Yahweh has removed men far away, and the forsaken places are many within the land.
If there is a tenth left in it, that also will in turn be consumed: as a terebinth, and as an oak, whose stock remains when they are felled; so the holy seed is its stock.”

footnotes.content: King Uzziah has died—a pillar of the earthly kingdom falls. But Isaiah enters the temple and sees what remains fixed: the Lord on His throne, high and lifted up. Sometimes we need the scaffolding of earthly certainties to crumble before we see what truly never shakes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six wings each: two to cover the face (reverence before holiness), two for the feet (humility), two for flight (readiness to serve). Even the highest creatures know their place before the King. There's deep instruction in how they stand—not in proud display, but in a servant's posture.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Holy, holy, holy—the repetition is no stammer. It breaks open the weight of what Isaiah is hearing. Every created thing in heaven and earth rings with the same refrain. When you finally hear holiness proclaimed truly, silence ceases and only one song fits.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The thresholds shake, smoke fills the house. Holiness is not tame. It moves the earth. Yet even in terror—the building still stands; the worship continues. God's presence shakes what deserves shaking but holds what must be held.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah cries out his unworthiness—not because he is unusually sinful, but because he has seen the King. One glimpse of true holiness undoes all pretense. The people around him are no better than he is, yet standing in this light, he cannot hide behind the crowd.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A seraph takes tongs and gathers a live coal from the altar—not to punish, but to heal. The same fire that burns unclean lips cleanses them. The Lord's answer to Isaiah's cry of despair is not words but an act of tender purification.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Your iniquity is taken away, your sin forgiven—the coal touches his mouth and speaks absolution. No penance, no earning it back. Just the touch of cleansing fire and the Word that makes it so. This is what it means to be forgiven in the presence of the Holy One.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord asks, Who will go for us? He does not command. He asks. And Isaiah, just moments ago undone and fearful, now hears the invitation and answers without hesitation: Here I am. Send me. Only a cleansed heart dares to volunteer for a prophet's lonely road.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You hear but don't understand; you see but don't perceive. Isaiah is being sent to a people whose ears and eyes are already sealed. It is not a sending toward easy harvest but toward apparent futility. Yet he goes anyway—because a true prophet speaks the Lord's word, not for the applause of listeners, but for the truth itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord's paradox: Go, make their hearts fat, their ears heavy, their eyes shut. Not that He takes pleasure in their blindness, but judgment itself can harden a rebellious heart. The people have already turned away; His word both summons and seals their refusal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah's first question—Lord, how long?—is also the prophet's eternal question. How long until the Lord acts? How long until justice comes? And the answer begins with desolation: cities waste, houses empty. The refining fire must burn away the dross first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judgment spans generations. The Lord removes people far away; the land fills with forsaken places. Isaiah sees not just discipline but the slow dissolution of those who would not listen. It is mercy offered and refused, again and again, until the land itself groans empty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this final word: even as the eighth falls, a tenth remains—a holy seed, a stump that will sprout again. We now know this seed bore fruit in Christ. In our own times of thinning and burning, we trust the same stubborn grace that preserves a remnant for resurrection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
